How toxins relate to each other beyond their taxonomy: which toxins look alike to a protein language model, and which molecular targets are hit independently by unrelated lineages.

A protein language model's learned embedding for every record in this dataset, reduced to 2D (UMAP). Where UniProt annotates a mature chain or peptide, that region was embedded (signal peptides and propeptides removed; multi-chain toxins as their chains joined); records with no such annotation were embedded in full. Each record’s detail panel states what was embedded. The embeddings were computed outside this page and supplied as coordinates. Fragment records (incomplete sequences) were embedded as deposited, so their positions may be less reliable. No human-assigned labels are involved: proximity reflects what the model considers similar, so toxins from unrelated lineages that land together are candidates for shared function or fold.
Top disagreements
Scroll to zoom, drag to pan. Hover a point to see what it is; click it to open that record. Choose Select (or hold Shift) and drag a box to list those toxins on the right — Shift+drag adds to the selection. Search highlights matches on the map; Enter zooms to them. CSV/FASTA export the selection (or everything if nothing is selected); SVG/PNG export the current view with its legend. Model agreement colors each toxin by how many of its 15 nearest neighbours are the same in both maps; low overlap means ProtT5 (sequence) and ProstT5 (structure-aware) disagree about what it resembles — candidates for fold-versus-sequence questions. Overlap is measured on the 2D UMAP coordinates, not the original embeddings, so some disagreement is projection noise. Tip: color by Disulfide pattern and compare ProtT5 vs ProstT5 — if same-colored points cluster in one but not the other, that's a real signal about fold (ProstT5) versus sequence (ProtT5).
Built from UniProt's own curated keywords rather than the embeddings: many venom targets are hit by toxins with completely unrelated protein folds — evolved independently, not inherited from a common ancestor. Click a target below to see which taxonomic groups and toxin classes converge on it.

How to read this — caveats
Values are parsed from free text that UniProt curators transcribed from the literature, so treat this as a starting point for literature review, not a validated cross-study ranking.

In vivo = LD50/PD50 from the “Toxic dose” field. Mass doses are converted to mg/kg-equivalent. Molar doses (such as nmol/g) are converted with the molecular weight of the stored mature chain and flagged “≈”, but are skipped for heterodimers and other multi-chain toxins, where one stored chain would give the wrong weight. Bounds (“>20 mg/kg”, “below 5 µg/kg”) are not treated as values. Doses in other units (µg/mL on cells, mouse units, per-insect amounts) are not parsed, so roughly 1 in 9 records that mention an LD50 are not listed here.

In vitro = IC50/EC50/Kd/Ki found in the function text, converted to nM. A list such as “IC50 of 369, 386 and 287 nM” is split into separate values, and a range keeps its lower end. Concentrations given as mass per volume (µg/mL) are not converted.

A record with several measurements is ranked by its lowest value — its best route or target, not an average. Routes, species, assay conditions and targets are not standardized across studies, and the target type tag (channel/receptor, enzyme, cell) is a keyword-based guess.

Checked: a 50-record spot check against the UniProt text (25 in vivo, 25 in vitro) found the parsed numbers correct in 48; the two errors (a “below” bound read as a value, and a heterodimer dose converted from one chain) are fixed, along with several wrong target-type tags. It is a sample, not a guarantee.

How to read this
Protein families with at least 12 characterized members. Position shows the share of members with an experimentally solved structure (PDB): families near the bottom, especially large ones at 0%, have no solved structure. Colour and the number on each card show how confident AlphaFold is about the members that are not solved: the mean pLDDT of their predicted models (>90 very high, 70–90 confident, 50–70 low, <50 very low). A family that is both unsolved and confidently modelled is where a prediction can stand in for an experiment today; an unsolved family with low confidence needs the experiment. The mean is shown only when at least 5 unsolved members have a model. pLDDT is computed over the whole translated precursor, including signal and propeptide regions (for 14 records AlphaFold modelled only part of the sequence, and only that part counts).

Each dot is one protein family. Height is the share of its members that are solved; colour is AlphaFold's mean confidence for the members that are not. Click a dot for the full family.

Clinically important species — toxin-record coverage

What this shows
What this shows. The WHO Guidelines for the production, control and regulation of snake antivenom immunoglobulins (Annex 5, TRS No. 1004) list the snake species of greatest medical importance in four broad world regions — the species responsible for the most frequent or severe snakebite envenoming, and the starting point for regional antivenom-production priorities. This view cross-references that list against this dataset by organism name, so you can see, region by region, which medically important species already have a characterized Tox-Prot venom proteome and which have no characterized toxin entries at all — a real, public-health-relevant venomics gap list, distinct from the Structural Gaps view in Insights. Species are matched by binomial name only; taxonomic synonyms or recent splits may occasionally cause a miss.

Disulfide bond landscape

What this page shows
Disulfide bond positions come straight from UniProt's curated Disulfide bond feature (not predicted). Cysteines are numbered within the mature chain only where that boundary is annotated (signal peptide/propeptide cysteines are excluded, since they're cleaved off before secretion and aren't part of the final toxin). For each entry with fully-paired cysteines, bonds are re-expressed as a connectivity pattern: cysteines are numbered 1, 2, 3… in sequence order, and each bond is written as a pair of those numbers — e.g. 1-4, 2-5, 3-6 for the classic three-disulfide inhibitor cystine knot (ICK/knottin) topology. Because this numbering ignores actual sequence position, the same pattern can show up in toxins from completely unrelated animals — spiders, cone snails, scorpions — which is usually a sign of convergent evolution onto the same stable disulfide-locked scaffold, not shared ancestry. Entries with an odd cysteine count, or where the curated bonds don't fully pair every cysteine within the mature chain, are shown separately since a pattern label isn't meaningful for them. Each pattern card below also shows how often it recurs and what share of its members have a solved structure — a pattern that's both common and well-characterized structurally (like ICK/knottin) is generally a safer bet as a drug-design scaffold than a rare, structurally unexplored one. You can also color the Embedding Map (Toxin Relationships) and the Taxonomy tree by disulfide pattern to see whether a scaffold clusters by sequence, by lineage, or both.

Most common connectivity patterns

Each card is one complete pattern: how all the cysteines of a toxin are paired, numbered in order along the mature chain. For example 1-4, 2-5, 3-6 means the 1st cysteine bonds to the 4th, the 2nd to the 5th and the 3rd to the 6th. The number on the card is how many toxins share that exact pattern.

Unpaired cysteine outliers

Entries where the curated disulfide bonds leave one or more cysteines unmatched — sometimes a free catalytic/reactive thiol, sometimes an intermolecular (inter-chain) bond to a different protein, occasionally just a curation gap. Worth a manual look before relying on these for framework classification.

How to read this
Built from NCBI's classification for each source organism, domain down to species. Use it to see how toxin coverage, structural data, and disulfide scaffolds are distributed across the animal kingdom — including cases where unrelated lineages (say, a spider and a cone snail) independently evolved the same disulfide scaffold. Long runs of single-child ancestry are compressed into one row, shown as a breadcrumb, so you're not scrolling through a dozen nested clades with nothing else branching off them.

About this atlas

The data
UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Tox-Prot

This atlas covers 8,274 reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot records of animal venom proteins, curated by Tox-Prot, UniProt's programme for animal toxins. 86% carry UniProt's “Toxin” keyword; the rest are mostly proteins expressed in the venom gland, such as hyaluronidases and phospholipases. Tox-Prot includes proteins from venomous animals such as snakes, spiders, scorpions, cone snails and centipedes, and from poisonous animals without a venom apparatus, such as some toads and ticks. Each record has the same curation standard as the rest of Swiss-Prot.

The data are a UniProt export from 26 Sep 2026 (Metazoa, taxonomy ID 33208), including InterPro cross-references. Every record links back to its UniProt entry, which remains the authoritative source.

What the atlas adds
views and values built on top of the records

Records can be browsed, filtered, compared and exported, and each tab gives a different view: organisms and their NCBI taxonomy, disulfide connectivity patterns, WHO-listed snakes, embedding maps and shared targets, statistics, structural gaps and potency, and a local Smith-Waterman similarity search.

Some values are worked out here and are not UniProt fields: the animal group (from the NCBI lineage), the toxin class (a grouping of UniProt protein families defined for this atlas; records with no family annotation have no class), disulfide connectivity patterns, potency and lethality (parsed from UniProt free text), computed sequence properties (pI, charge, GRAVY; calculated from the stored sequence, without cleavage or modifications), and the AlphaFold and embedding summaries below.

AlphaFold confidence
AlphaFold DB, model version 6, retrieved 12 Oct 2026

Per-residue pLDDT comes from AlphaFold DB and is shown as a strip on each record's sequence map, in Statistics and in Structural Gaps. The bands follow AlphaFold's own: above 90 very high, 70–90 confident, 50–70 low, below 50 very low. Means cover the sequence AlphaFold modelled, usually the whole precursor, so signal and propeptide regions are included. Records with a solved structure still show the strip, because solved structures usually cover only the mature toxin.

Embedding maps
ProtT5 and ProstT5, projected with UMAP

The two maps in Toxin Relationships use protein language model embeddings of each record's mature region (ProtT5 for sequence, ProstT5 as a structure-aware model), reduced to two dimensions with UMAP (n_neighbors 15, min_dist 0.1, random_state 42). They were computed outside this page. Cluster shapes and distances are not quantitative, and the nearest-neighbour and model-agreement views are measured on these 2D coordinates, so they are approximate.

WHO medically important snakes
a second data source

Records whose organism matches a species in the WHO snake antivenom guidelines (Annex 5, TRS No. 1004, Tables A5.3–A5.6) carry a WHO badge, filterable in Browse and broken down by subregion in Clinical Importance. Species are matched by binomial name only. The list is WHO's, not a Tox-Prot annotation.

How to cite
the atlas, its data, and the methods behind it

If this atlas helps your work, please cite the underlying resources — UniProt and the Tox-Prot programme first and foremost — and mention the atlas itself:

Lingappa, S. (2026). Animal Toxin Atlas: an interactive browser for UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Tox-Prot animal toxin records. Data: UniProt Tox-Prot export, retrieved September 2026.
